gdp.quote: Between July and September, the economy expanded by 0.7%, accelerating from the three months previously, official figures show. […] Within services, computer programming registered its fastest growth for the past three years, helped by AI linked spending.

gdp.title: Ignore the rate rise, worry about the forecast
gdp.quote: The bigger story this week wasn’t the rate rise, it was the Bank’s new economic outlook. Inflation is now forecast to peak at 4.9 per cent next spring and not to get back to the 2 per cent target until the third quarter of 2028. That’s a full two years later than the Bank expected back in the halcyon days of February. […] And getting inflation down won’t come cheap. In the Bank’s forecast, it hikes interest rates to nearly 5 per cent (although it has been at pains to stress that this is not a guide to future policy). Higher rates mean that growth is now expected to average a feeble 1.1 per cent annual pace over the next two years. More inflation and less growth add up to a nasty outlook for pay. Private-sector earnings are forecast to fall by 0.5 per cent in real terms next year, meaning the average worker in 2027 is set to be paid £390 less in real terms than they were in 2025.

unemp.title: It’s good to be flexible
unemp.quote: If the LPC had done something similar this year – continued closing the gap to the adult rate, with a target of 2029 – then the 18-20-year-old rate would have increased by roughly 10 per cent. But the Government has responded to flashing alarm bells in the youth labour market by relaxing (or clarifying) this part of the LPC’s remit too. The LPC was told explicitly it could choose the pace of the youth-adult convergence (i.e. ‘don’t fixate on 2029’) and that it should prioritise young people’s employment prospects. […] I thought this might lead to some convergence, albeit less than in recent years, resulting in a youth uprating just above the adult uprating. But the LPC paused convergence altogether. I think this was a good call. As I set out last week, we can’t say for sure that minimum wage increases are to blame for a deteriorating youth labour market, but we also can’t say that they are not, and it’s not worth taking the risk.

unemp.title: The Budget should not price young people out of work
unemp.quote: John Healey is about to deliver his first Budget, and the first fiscal event of Andy Burnham’s premiership. unemp.title: The Budget should not price young people out of work
unemp.quote: If you raise the price of a worker whose tasks a machine can do, some of that work can move to the machine. In 2017 it was older factory workers. In 2026 it is younger professional workers, and also possibly school leavers on tills and counters that self-service machines can replace. In fact, the Bank of England’s agents report warehouse operators looking to automate after recent labour cost inflation, and retail and hospitality have shed 117,000 employees in a year, more than all other industries combined. Out-of-work benefit claims have risen most among 18 to 20-year-olds, from 7.2 to 9.4 per cent between 2022 and 2025. Meanwhile the 18 to 20 minimum wage rate has risen 45 per cent in three years, from £7.49 to £10.85, taking it from 72 to 85 per cent of the adult rate. A price rise of that size, for workers who have just become substitutable, lies outside anything in the Commission’s known evidence base.

unemp.title: Is the minimum wage to blame for falling youth employment?
unemp.quote: Employment rates among 18-24 and 25-64-year-olds fully recovered after Covid, but the trend for young people then diverged. The youth employment rate fell from 2022 onwards, now standing almost 6 per cent below 2019 levels. By contrast, the rate among 25-64-year-olds held up, reached a new high in 2023, and only then drifted down to 1 per cent below 2019 levels. So, the picture is pretty much the same as where we started. There has been a serious fall in youth employment since 2022, which isn’t accounted for by rising education participation, or by population or migration changes.

unemp.title: Is the minimum wage to blame for falling youth employment?
unemp.quote: What if this is all structural change, not policy? Perhaps the shape of the economy shifted against the young. Retail and wholesale jobs never recovered post-Covid and have been falling since 2022, while hospitality jobs have fallen since 2023. Together those sectors account for 2-in-5 youth jobs, and they stopped adding jobs just as more young people needed work. You can tell a story of big forces here: online shopping; automated warehouses; and a preference for screens to seeing our mates.

pop.title: Does falling migration spell trouble for the Budget?
pop.quote: Our data and knowledge is simply not good enough to be very confident about the fiscal consequences of the recent reductions in net migration. The £7bn cost is almost certainly a large over-estimate and it is conceivable there is actually a benefit. Even if the reductions in net migration have a small fiscal cost over the forecast horizon they are of migrants who, on average, are likely to be fiscally negative over their lifetime. Immigration of this type is akin to borrowing – it gives you more resources today at the expense of less in the future. Where fiscal rules constrain literal borrowing this migration as disguised borrowing has been an attractive policy for successive governments. But this would not be the first government if it succumbed to the temptations of short-termism.

pop.title: Does falling migration spell trouble for the Budget?
pop.quote: The March 2024 OBR estimates also do not take into account who the migrants are, how much they work and how much they earn. They assume migrants are the same as the average Brit of the same age and sex (broadly consistent with the data we have). But migrants vary a lot in their employment and earnings, so it’s important to think about the types of migrants that make up the reduction in net migration. The big reductions in migration have come from falls in care workers and their dependents, the dependents of Masters’ students, some family, nurses, and some other work migrants (mostly the lower-paid). Since the 2024 OBR report we know the first three groups have low levels of earnings, in some cases not much above minimum wage and that lower-paid migrants are more likely to stay. Taking account of this would again reduce the cost of the reduction in migration, though how much is uncertain, given the data. What’s more, nurses’ salaries are paid by the Government, so there is an extra expenditure associated with them.

pop.title: Does falling migration spell trouble for the Budget?
pop.quote: First, the OBR itself came to recognise that migration required more public expenditure that its March 2024 estimates implied if it was not to have some implicit austerity. In their September 2024 Fiscal risks and sustainability report, the OBR argued that extra public investment of £20k per person would be needed to maintain the public sector capital stock (the hospitals, schools roads etc) in per capita terms (though they also gave some reasons why this might be too high). But if migration is 100k lower for 5 years, then the saving from lower required public sector investment would be £10bn(100k migrants requires investment of £2bn, multiplied by 5 years) – i.e. this could conceivably wipe out the £7bn cost in the March 2024 estimates. At the very least it substantially reduces it.

earn.title: Budget 2026 special
earn.quote: The most disappointing thing about this Budget was what it told us about the long-run prospects for living standards. Real household disposable income per person is set to grow by just 0.1 per cent a year on average between 2019 and 2029, compared with 0.9 per cent between 2007 and 2019 and 2.4 per cent in the decade to 2007. TOTC readers will no doubt be familiar with the role economic growth (the blue bars) played in our post financial crisis disappointment. That it’s become relatively more expensive to buy things from the rest of the world (the yellow bars) also matters. But the 2020s squeeze on living standards has a new source (the red bar in the chart below): net taxes and benefits, which added to income growth after the financial crisis, are now a drag on it.

earn.title: My final newsletter – fewer meetings, less management, slower pay growth?
earn.quote: It wouldn’t be a Mike TOTC without some mention of inequality, and yesterday’s ONS Annual Survey of Hours and Earnings data dump gave us the definitive take on earnings inequality, with data now up to 2026. The headline was that the share of workers in low pay failed to fall for the first time in 15 years, but Chart of the Week takes a closer look at overall pay inequality, measured by the 90:10 ratio (where higher numbers mean more unequal pay) for hourly pay and weekly earnings. Women’s weekly earnings have long been less equal than men’s – due to their higher share of part-time workers – but the genders have been slowly converging since this series began in 2002. More recently, overall earnings inequality has ticked up across the board, after a decade of decline. This is partly because the National Living Wage, which used to outpace median pay, is now only keeping pace with it, but is also because high earners are pulling away: weekly pay for the 90th percentile grew by 7.3 per cent in nominal terms this year (to reach £1,433 a week), against just 1.1 per cent at the 10th percentile. Among men, earnings inequality is now at its joint highest on record (alongside 2014), thanks to increasing numbers with a low weekly paycheck (the 10th percentile fell in cash terms from £309 in 2025 to £301 in 2026).

gilt.title: How Is The UK’s Deficit Reduction Plan (Actually) Likely To Proceed?
gilt.quote: In this week’s blog, I set out what I think is a credible path for the UK’s public finances. I use the historical record of borrowing forecasts against outturns to discipline how the fiscal plans are likely to be revised in the years ahead. On this path, the primary balance improves but stays in deficit over the next five years. The current budget is in deficit by around £30 billion in 2029-30, so the fiscal rules are missed by a significant margin. The debt ratio rises throughout the forecast, reaching 101 per cent of GDP by 2031-32. My guess is that this is closer to the market’s expectation than the official forecast, and it may help resolve the puzzle of why the UK’s borrowing costs remain the highest in the G7 despite the IMF’s praise.

gas.title: Budget 2026 special
gas.quote: One of the Chancellor’s big choices was to use some of his insurance policy (letting the current budget that he has promised to balance fall from £24bn to £15bn). If things turn out better than expected this will prove a wise move. So far, however, it looks like the Chancellor’s chips are down. The OBR took economic data up to mid-August into account in its forecast. By Budget day, gas prices were far above the OBR’s central forecast and looked dangerously close to its “severe” shock scenario, while oil had climbed two-thirds of the way there. On energy prices, the OBR’s downside scenario is starting to look like the central case (though at our event this week Haskel explained that how long high prices are sustained for will be crucial). In that scenario, inflation tops 5 per cent next year. But the Government does get a sliver of good news. Although the severe scenario does show higher borrowing overall, that’s entirely down to a one percentage point rise in gilt yields that has not yet materialised. So while households are facing something like the severe scenario, the Treasury (for now at least) is not.

gas.title: What does the abolition of the gas standing charge mean for households?
gas.quote: While the £100 Household Energy Payment grabbed most of the headlines, another energy bill change announced on Wednesday has got less attention. But John Healey’s request for Ofgem to abolish the standing charge on household gas bills by the end of 2027 will also affect future bills. And because it’s a regulatory change, the Treasury leaves it out of its distributional analysis. So here we’ve tried to fill that gap and understand who will win – and lose – from this switch. […] The standing charge, £108 a year for the typical billpayer, is paid by every gas-connected household however little gas it uses. Suppliers will recover it through higher unit rates instead, so the change costs the Exchequer nothing, and efforts to reduce the disparity between gas and electricity costs will – in a small way – help to make the case for more heat pumps in homes. […] But it is not free: it moves around £600 million a year from households that use more gas to those that use less, with no regard to their incomes. In effect, it adds to what we at RF have dubbed the “shadow tax and benefit system hidden within energy bills”, with the transfer set by a regulator rather than in a Budget.

ecb.title: Ahead of a presidential election, France first needs to help itself on debt
ecb.quote: Of all the sovereigns facing rising rates, France may face the biggest challenge. Today’s bond market is exposing a French economic problem that has been building for years. France has lost economic ground relative to Germany since about 2010, in a context of Germany’s own weak performance. More strikingly, France has lost ground relative to Italy since 2020 (Figure 1). France must grapple with structurally higher long-term interest rates in the context of a very weak fiscal starting point and a longstanding growth problem. Until now, French government bonds have enjoyed something close to a mini-exorbitant privilege, with yields just a little higher than Germany and in any case too big to fail. Public debt climbed from around the Maastricht-compatible 60 percent of GDP at the birth of the euro to 120 percent today, without governments being forced to confront the sustainability of public debt and the French social model.

In contrast, the physical economy, including agriculture, extraction, and construction, is expected to see minimal growth—less than 1% in agriculture and only 3% in both extraction and construction. These sectors face challenges due to their reliance on manual, on-site work, limiting AI’s impact.

The report highlights that the 2030s will be pivotal, with substantial productivity gains anticipated as AI adoption becomes mainstream. Financial and business services are expected to lead this growth, while sectors like manufacturing and agriculture may lag behind, with less than half of their projected gains realised by 2035.

tfp.title: The 2026 Budget buys stability and points in the right direction on growth
tfp.quote: Growth is what generates the tax receipts to stabilise public finances and raise living standards. The UK economy has shown resilience, with growth ranking top of the G7 in the first half of the year. Recent productivity data restatements imply that our post financial crisis slowdown was less bad than previously thought, but there’s still significant slowdown that must be addressed. The uptick in productivity (per worker) that we have seen since Q3 2024 suggests that this is possible if business investment is encouraged and confidence maintained.

tfp.title: Does falling migration spell trouble for the Budget?
tfp.quote: The OBR estimates may also be optimistic in their baseline assumption that investment responds positively to higher migration, leaving the long-run capital-labour ratio unaffected. If this was right, we should be in the middle of an investment boom right now – net migration was about 2.5 per cent of population in 2021/23 – if the capital-output ratio is about 4 this requires extra investment of 10 per cent of GDP to maintain the capital labour ratio. But we do not seem to be experiencing an investment boom. The latest flash productivity estimates show productivity per worker falling in the period of very high net migration and now growing again with lower migration. Some commentators are arguing that higher productivity growth is because of the type of reductions in migration– I don’t think we have enough evidence to be so confident but it is an argument that needs to be taken seriously and, if true, also implies that the fiscal cost of reductions in net migration is much lower than thought, perhaps not negative at all.

fiscal.title: How Is The UK’s Deficit Reduction Plan (Actually) Likely To Proceed?
fiscal.quote: This week’s Budget, like its predecessors, assumes a sizeable fiscal squeeze in the years ahead. On the OBR’s numbers, the primary balance (tax receipts minus spending on everything except debt interest) is forecast to improve by 3 per cent of GDP over the next 5 years, from a deficit of 1.5 per cent in 2025-26 to a surplus of the same size by 2030-31. The IMF singled the UK out this month as one of the few advanced economies where action on the deficit has been taken decisively. […] The trouble is that few people outside the Fund expect this squeeze to be delivered. Most of the tightening is scheduled for 2029-30, which could well be the run-up to the next election. This is the familiar pattern of promising fiscal prudence tomorrow, what Charlie Bean once called the “Augustinian approach” to fiscal policy.

fiscal.title: How Is The UK’s Deficit Reduction Plan (Actually) Likely To Proceed?
fiscal.quote: In this week’s blog, I set out what I think is a credible path for the UK’s public finances. I use the historical record of borrowing forecasts against outturns to discipline how the fiscal plans are likely to be revised in the years ahead. On this path, the primary balance improves but stays in deficit over the next five years. The current budget is in deficit by around £30 billion in 2029-30, so the fiscal rules are missed by a significant margin. The debt ratio rises throughout the forecast, reaching 101 per cent of GDP by 2031-32. My guess is that this is closer to the market’s expectation than the official forecast, and it may help resolve the puzzle of why the UK’s borrowing costs remain the highest in the G7 despite the IMF’s praise.

fiscal.title: Budget 2026 special
fiscal.quote: One of the Chancellor’s big choices was to use some of his insurance policy (letting the current budget that he has promised to balance fall from £24bn to £15bn). If things turn out better than expected this will prove a wise move. So far, however, it looks like the Chancellor’s chips are down. The OBR took economic data up to mid-August into account in its forecast. By Budget day, gas prices were far above the OBR’s central forecast and looked dangerously close to its “severe” shock scenario, while oil had climbed two-thirds of the way there. On energy prices, the OBR’s downside scenario is starting to look like the central case (though at our event this week Haskel explained that how long high prices are sustained for will be crucial). In that scenario, inflation tops 5 per cent next year. But the Government does get a sliver of good news. Although the severe scenario does show higher borrowing overall, that’s entirely down to a one percentage point rise in gilt yields that has not yet materialised. So while households are facing something like the severe scenario, the Treasury (for now at least) is not.

fiscal.title: Breathing Space, Not a Strategy
fiscal.quote: Today’s Budget has seen the Chancellor deliver some ‘breathing space’ to households struggling with cost-of-living pressures via a mild fiscal loosening, most obviously through changes to energy bills and council taxes. Against an already difficult domestic and international macroeconomic backdrop, which has created a strain on the public finances, the net effect of today’s measures has been a reduction in the Chancellor’s buffer against his fiscal rules from £23.6 billion in March to £14.5 billion now. Market reaction to the Budget was subsequently muted. Ten-year gilt yields fell by only a few basis points on Wednesday afternoon, while sterling hardly budged. […] Therefore, while today’s Budget appears to have not resulted in a backlash from the markets, maintaining a backloaded path for tax rises and deferring major fiscal decisions on defence and other spending until the 2027 Spending Review to buy time is not a credible fiscal strategy.

fiscal.title: Breathing Space, Not a Strategy
fiscal.quote: The OBR forecasts that policies announced in this budget will lead to increased borrowing over the next three years of £12.4 billion, which will then be followed by a reduction of £7 billion on average in the years after. Based on the forecast paths laid out by the OBR today we can see that our minimal test of credibility was not met with Public Sector Net Debt peaking at around 97 per cent of GDP in 2028-29 before falling only slightly to 96 per cent of GDP in 2031-32, higher than the ratio in August this year of 94 per cent.

fiscal.title: John Healey’s underwhelming budget punts big decisions into 2027
fiscal.quote: Many small changes could have cumulated to a big overall change in fiscal stance. But they mostly cancelled out. On the forecast, the cost to the exchequer from slightly lower real growth is offset by higher tax receipts, helped in large part by tax thresholds remaining frozen. Higher interest rates means forecast borrowing increased, and Healey allowed the bigger fiscal buffer Reeves had built up to fall to absorb that shock. That leaves him only a 56% chance, based on past forecast errors, of meeting his main fiscal rule of a current budget surplus in 2029/30, down from 59% at the last budget.

tariff.title: What a Democratic Congress Means for Federal Tax Policy in 2027
tariff.quote: Some Democratic policymakers have opposed the Trump administration’s imposition of hundreds of billions of dollars in tariffs, and have pledged to vote to roll them back. The issue doesn’t split neatly along party lines, though. […] Many Democrats oppose the way President Trump imposed tariffs—unilaterally, on wide swaths of goods, and on economic adversaries and allies alike, with rapid, chaotic changes. However, some support tariffs on specific goods, such as aluminum and steel. Even if Democrats muster the votes to roll back some or all of Trump’s tariffs, it’s unlikely Congress could assemble a veto-proof majority on the issue in the next two years.

tariff.title: The UK-EU summit will be a test of the political salience of Brexit
tariff.quote: Since the initial Common Understanding was agreed, a new problem has emerged for the prime minister – the risk to UK manufacturing supply chains of the EU’s more protectionist Made in Europe stance. This is not aimed at the UK – but it risks being collateral damage unless the prime minister can convince the EU that the UK (and potentially other third country trade partners too) should sneak inside the EU’s protective wall. But that will not be costless. A proposal from German chancellor Friedrich Merz and French president Emmanuel Macron would see the UK exempted from Made in Europe restrictions on cars, provided it agreed to align its external tariff with the EU’s to prevent it being a backdoor route for Chinese EVs into the EU.

tariff.title: US inflation higher than expected in October - here's what is happening with prices
tariff.quote: Higher tariffs - which are levies that businesses pay on the goods they import - directly raise prices for US companies unless the overseas firms they are buying from lower prices to absorb some of the cost. […] In response to the new tariffs, the New York Fed found exporters reduced prices very little, meaning US-based businesses ended up absorbing nearly 90% of the cost of the added tax. […] Indirectly, higher tariffs also affected the prices of locally made goods, as many US producers rely on parts or materials from overseas. […] Overall, the Fed found that every percentage point increase in average tariffs led to nearly a 0.25% price increase for consumer goods after one year.

Overall, the Fed found that every percentage point increase in average tariffs led to nearly a 0.25% price increase for consumer goods after one year.
